slides.0.title: Industry, market and Diploma essays
slides.0.subtitle: Producer structure, exports and price bands, plus blind-tasting clues and MW-style essay examples
slides.1.title: Exports and markets
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Exports are falling
slides.1.highlights.0.content: 2025 exports were €555 million (-12%) and 1.8 million hl (-9%), less than half of 2020's 3.8 million hl; 2022 was €773 million (Meininger, citing I numeri del vino / UN Comtrade)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Mostly bottled
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Bottled wine is about 90% of export revenue; bulk is only about €33 million
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Main markets (volume)
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The UK first, the USA second, Brazil third and Canada fourth (2025); Malbec was 69.3% of exported varietal volume in 2023 (INV)
slides.1.content: Argentine exports lean on Malbec and a few markets, and both volume and value have shrunk in recent years.
slides.2.title: Price bands and positioning
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Mid-shelf brand Malbec
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Malbec built a global mid-shelf brand with consistent ripe fruit at accessible prices (WSET study material)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: High-altitude icon wines
slides.2.highlights.1.content: High-altitude icon wines aim at critical scores and higher price points
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Producer structure
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Large groups sit alongside family and boutique estates; detailed market shares must be checked in official reports and are not quoted here
slides.2.content: Argentina has a lot of mid-priced Malbec and a little high-altitude icon wine, and the two ends run on different logic.
slides.3.title: Blind-tasting clues and an essay outline
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Tasting clues
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Malbec: violet, black and blue fruit, plush tannin; Uco: fresh, chalky, bright acidity; Luján: structured; Torrontés: rose, geranium, peach; Patagonian Pinot: cool and fresh
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Essay outline: altitude
slides.3.highlights.1.content: 1) Thesis: altitude is Argentina's most important terroir variable; 2) Mechanism: cooling, day-night swing, UV, acidity; 3) Examples: Luján vs Uco vs Cafayate; 4) Risks and limits: frost, heat, water; 5) Conclusion
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Exam reminder
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Discuss both the mechanism and its limits; Patagonia, cool from latitude rather than altitude, is a good counter-example
slides.3.content: An MW-style essay needs a thesis, mechanism, examples, limits and a conclusion.
slides.4.title: Diploma depth: collapsing home consumption and macroeconomics
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The long fall in per-capita consumption
slides.4.highlights.0.content: In 1970 Argentines drank about 90 litres per head a year; INV data put 2025 at a record low of about 15.8 litres, against about 29 litres in 2005. Explanations vary: falling purchasing power, health awareness, zero-tolerance drink-driving rules (reported figures not tested)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Causal chain: shrinking home market → industry change
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The industry once relied on a huge domestic bulk market; as it shrank → surplus cheap wine, high-yielding Criolla varieties uprooted → a 1990s turn to quality and exports. This explains Mendoza’s sharp loss of area in 1980–2003 and the rise of Malbec exports
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Exchange rates and inflation
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The big peso devaluation of 2002 made export prices highly competitive, driving investment and tourism; but persistent high inflation drives up local costs, and if the exchange rate does not adjust in step, exporters’ margins are squeezed. Macroeconomic instability is the hardest variable for Argentine wine to control
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Essay language
slides.4.highlights.3.content: “Argentina’s terroir advantages are stable; its economic environment is not”: in industry questions, assess natural conditions (altitude, dryness) separately from institutional and economic ones (exchange rates, home demand, export reliance on Malbec)
slides.4.content: The key to Argentine industry questions: collapsing home demand drove the quality turn, and macroeconomics decides export success.
slides.5.title: Short-answer practice: question and marking points
slides.5.highlights.0.title: Question 1
slides.5.highlights.0.content: “Compare Malbec from Luján de Cuyo and the Uco Valley and explain the reasons for their differences in style.” (about 250 words)
slides.5.highlights.1.title: Marking points for question 1
slides.5.highlights.1.content: ① altitude: Luján about 800–1,100 m, Uco about 900–1,700 m and above; ② temperature and diurnal range → Uco keeps acidity and florality; ③ soil: stony, sandy alluvial fans in Luján, calcareous caliche in Uco → chalky tannins; ④ style: Luján classic and firmly structured, Uco fresh and mineral; ⑤ history and investment: Luján the traditional heart, Uco developed by foreign capital after the 1990s
slides.5.highlights.2.title: Question 2
slides.5.highlights.2.content: “Assess the risks and opportunities of Argentina’s heavy reliance on Malbec.” (about 350 words)
slides.5.highlights.3.title: Marking points for question 2
slides.5.highlights.3.content: ① current position: Malbec about 69.3% of varietal export volume (2023, INV); ② opportunities: strong national recognition, a full price ladder from mid-priced brands to high-altitude single sites; ③ risks: the category losing fashion, falling export volume and value, macroeconomic volatility; ④ diversification: Cabernet Franc, Bonarda, Torrontés, Patagonian Pinot Noir, sparkling; ⑤ conclude with a balanced verdict
slides.5.content: Write comparison answers side by side: cover both regions in each point rather than one paragraph each.
About what share of Argentina's 2025 export revenue came from bottled wine?
Which was the second-largest market by volume for Argentine exports in 2025?
The USA; the UK was first and Brazil third.
Why is Patagonia a good counter-example in an essay on altitude?
A. Its coolness comes from latitude and wind, not altitude
